Changing the dossier changed the absolute-score leader; pairwise judging restored Countermand. With facts only and bare forms checked, Claustra Labs topped 6 of 8 absolute-score rounds and Countermand Labs only 1. In head-to-head finals, judged in both orders, Countermand Labs won clearly on both Bradley–Terry (0.24 against 0.20 for Seneschal Labs) and Copeland (38 points against 29.5). The two names are close; which one wins depends on the scoring format.

Personas helped a little; temperature did not. Personas cut judge correlation on clear names from 0.75 to 0.71 (effective judges from 1.29 to 1.36) and made repeats slightly more stable (τ 0.93 against 0.89). Varied temperature lowered correlation marginally but made the two repeats disagree about the winner. This matches the literature: prompt and model diversity beat sampling diversity.

PeerRank weighting behaved as designed and changed almost nothing. The judges whose own names scored best (DeepSeek V4 Pro, Nemotron, DeepSeek V4 Flash: 0.16 each) gained power, and Claude Haiku 4.5, whose names scored worst, fell to 0.015. Yet the weighted ranking correlated 0.97 with the unweighted one and changed the top name in 1 of 8 rounds. When judges agree this much, reweighting them cannot add information. Reliability weighting moved even less (τ 0.997).

Pairwise judgements are noisy. 37% of a judge's verdicts on a pair flipped when the two names swapped positions, and judges leaned slightly towards whichever name was shown first (+0.04). Asking once per pair would be close to a coin toss for close names; judging both orders and treating flips as ties is necessary, not optional.

Optimising against Jev did not work, and Jev already agreed with the panel. Across five generate-and-score rounds (434 names), Jev's average stayed flat at 5.7–5.9, and its best score came in round 1 (Franklin Gate, 6.99). Bare Countermand scored 7.07, higher than every generated name. Jev compresses its scores and rewards easy, plain names (Keyhold, Latchkey, Quietgate), so the league winner is also Jev's favourite.

A fairer rematch against Jev confirmed it: the ceiling is Countermand. With pairwise questions, thinking switched on and ten fixed styles, 320 new names over five rounds never pulled clearly ahead. The best, Precept, would beat Countermand only 57% of the time, and the typical new name only 33%. Rounds did not improve: the best new name's chance fell from 58% in round 2 to 52% in round 5, and the generator ran short of fresh ideas (100 new names in round 1, 38 in round 5). Jev was far more order-consistent than the LLM panel (11% flips against 37%), but a third of its answers sat between 0.4 and 0.6. Latin and Greek borrowings and British legal terms did best; Banks-style phrases and plain words with a suffix did worst. Of the ten leaders, only Permissa, Wardence and Selden are clear at Companies House, and Precept, Phylax, Mandatum and Binnacle are blocked.
Total spend for everything was about $8.70, or £6.55. That covers the v1 league ($7.04), the v2 tests ($1.63) and the probes. The virtual key capped spend at $12 throughout and expires on 1 October.
